# Scan the Horizon (scanthehorizon.app)

> Scan the Horizon is a free web page for phones that names what you can see from where you stand. It draws the hills, mountains and coast around you the way the sign at a lookout does, in grey layers, and names the towns, cities, peaks, islands, lakes, lighthouses and other landmarks on the horizon in ovals with leader lines, each with how far away it is. Hold the phone up and the drawing turns with you; tap a name for its height or population, which way it is, and a link to Wikipedia. A Detail slider chooses how many names to show, and a List gives them all in order of bearing.

How it works: the page downloads elevation tiles for the land around you, out to 150 km (250 km near high mountains), from Mapterhorn (Copernicus GLO-30 worldwide, with finer national data such as Geoscience Australia's 5 m LiDAR and swissALTI3D), or from the AWS terrain tiles if Mapterhorn doesn't answer. In a background thread it marches out along every bearing to find the skyline and the ridges in front of it, allowing for the curve of the Earth and for refraction. Place names come from GeoNames, served by the site itself as small tiles; each place is checked against the terrain in front of it, so only what could really be seen is named, and a big place hidden behind a hill gets an arrow over the hill that hides it ("behind the hills", or "over the horizon" where only the curve of the Earth hides it). The terrain is the shape of the land rather than what stands on it (bare ground where there are detailed national surveys), so the view is drawn as if trees and buildings were glass, and it works indoors. The phone's compass is corrected from magnetic to true north with the World Magnetic Model 2025; without a compass, or on a computer, you drag to look around. A Camera button shows the drawing over the live camera picture, at true scale.

Privacy: your exact position stays on the phone. To draw a view the page downloads elevation tiles for the area around you and place names from this site, so those servers can tell roughly where you are and see your IP address. A place typed into the search is sent to Photon (komoot) or Open-Meteo. Links carry the place rounded to about 1 km unless the exact one is chosen. No cookies, no accounts.

Install: an installable app (PWA). Once opened, the page works offline, and views already opened can be drawn again without signal. To use it somewhere with no signal, save the area first (in the place sheet: within 2, 5, 10 or 20 km of a place); it stays on the phone until deleted. Looking from anywhere else needs a connection.

Technical: static files only (index.html, xray.css, app.js and draw.js for the page and the drawing, a module worker xray-worker.js with dem.js, decode.js, pano.js and targets.js for the terrain and the names, orientation.js for the compass, geocode.js for the place search), MIT-licensed code, no framework, no build step, no backend. "xray" in the file names is the project's working title.

## Links

- [Scan the Horizon](https://scanthehorizon.app/): the page itself; its About sheet explains how it works and answers questions (what it does, how it knows what is on the horizon, accuracy, privacy, offline use)
